title: Order Flow Imbalance and Short-Horizon FX Returns: A Multiple-Testing-Corrected Double Machine Learning Analysis
abstract: Order flow imbalance (OFI) has a long lineage in market microstructure as a candidate driver of short-horizon price impact, from Kyle's (1985) linear price-impact model through the bulk volume classification tradition underlying VPIN (Easley, López de Prado &amp; O'Hara, 2012). Practitioner claims that a given order-flow construction "predicts" returns are common but are rarely subjected to a causal standard that separates a structural relationship from confounding by time-of-day, volatility clustering, and recent momentum — nor to correction for the fact that testing many instruments and time partitions inflates the chance of a false positive. This note applies Double Machine Learning (Chernozhukov et al., 2018) to a transparent, bar-level OFI proxy across a systematic 32-instrument, 730,013-observation sweep of 30-minute FX, metals, and sovereign-bond-CFD data, and subjects the resulting 256-test battery to Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Under the correction family appropriate to a single pre-specified sweep, no instrument-session pairing retains a statistically defensible relationship between OFI and 90-minute forward returns. A small number of nominally significant results survive a looser, per-instrument correction, but carry effect sizes too small to be economically meaningful. The result is reported as a genuine null: a signal that would appear promising under the single-pair, uncorrected screen many practitioner claims rely on does not survive a stricter, causally motivated, multiple-testing-aware test.
